title: The People of the Book
hookLine: the Qur'an speaks to Jews and Christians as people of scripture, with praise and with argument (2:62; 3:113–114)

cards: Medina, in the time of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, wasn't a town of one faith. Jewish tribes had their own neighborhoods, markets and scholars. Christians came too: once, from Najran, as a delegation that stayed to talk.
The Qur'an had a name for all of them, and it wasn't stranger or outsider. It was a name about a book. Ahl al-kitab.
The family, or the people, of the scripture.

teach.b: Ahl means family, household, people. Kitab is book, scripture. The name starts from what they share with Muslims: a revealed book, Torah and Gospel among the scriptures the Qur'an honors.
The Qur'an speaks to them in two voices, and it's honest to hear both. Praise first.
Surah three, verses one thirteen and one fourteen: they are not all alike.
Among the people of the scripture is an upright community who recite Allah's verses through the night and bow down, who believe and do good and hurry to it.
Al-Baqarah, verse sixty-two, names believers, Jews, Christians and Sabaeans: whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day and does right has their reward with their Lord.
Muslim scholars read that verse more narrowly or more broadly, and the debate is old. Then argument.

The Qur'an disputes with Jews and Christians over points of belief, such as who 'Isa was, and it criticizes some of their conduct in its time. It doesn't hide that. But it also sets the manner of the argument.
Surah three invites them to a common word: that we worship only Allah.

teach.h: ARGUE ONLY IN THE BEST WAY.
teach.b: Surah twenty-nine: don't argue with the people of the scripture except in the best way. And surah five allows Muslims to eat their food, and Muslim men to marry their women.
Praise, argument, a shared table. Jews and Christians, of course, describe their own faiths in their own words. This is how the Qur'an speaks to them.

how: Muslims use ahl al-kitab for Jews and Christians (and some scholars for others with scripture); classical Islamic law permits eating their food and allows Muslim men to marry Jewish and Christian women, and 29:46 is often quoted on respectful dialogue.

games.q: a Christian or Jewish neighbor disagrees with you about faith. what manner does surah twenty-nine set?
o: argue only in the best way.
games.why: don't argue with the people of the scripture except in the best way (29:46).

practice: Think of a Jewish or Christian person you know, a congregation you pass, or any faith not your own, and notice what you actually know about how they pray or what they read. Notice the gaps without judging them.
Then pick one question you'd honestly like answered, by them or by a source of their own, not by someone talking about them.

wordCard.voice: Ahl al-kitab. People of the book, the Qur'an's name for Jews and Christians: spoken to with praise, with argument, and in the best way. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: people of the book, people of scripture.

carryVoice: Your line: people of the book. A shared scripture, and the best way to argue. That's a week, done.
